Title: Lung cancer.
Abstract: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related mortality. Since tobacco smoking is the cause in vast majority of cases, the incidence of lung cancer is expected to rise in those countries with high or rising incidence of tobacco smoking. Even though populations at risk of developing lung cancer are easily identified, mass screening for lung cancer is not supported by currently available evidence. In the case of non-small cell lung cancer, a cure may be possible with surgical resection followed by post-operative chemotherapy in those diagnosed at an early stage. A small minority of patients who present with locally advanced disease may also benefit from pre-operative chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy to down stage the tumor to render it potentially operable. In a vast majority of patients, however, lung cancer presents at an advanced stage and a cure is not possible with currently available therapeutic strategies. Similarly, small cell lung cancer confined to one hemi-thorax may be curable with a combination of chemotherapy and thoracic irradiation followed by prophylactic cranial irradiation, if complete remission is achieved at the primary site. Small cell lung cancer that is spread beyond the confines of one hemi-thorax is, however, considered incurable. In this era of molecular targeted therapies, new agents are constantly undergoing pre-clinical and clinical testing with the aim of targeting the molecular pathways thought be involved in etiology and pathogenesis of lung cancer.
Abstract_Summary: This research looks at lung cancer, which is the top cause of death from cancer (Abstract, sentence 1). We need this study because many people smoke, and in places where more people smoke, more people will get lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 2). You may know who is at high risk, like long term smokers, but we still do not have proof that testing everyone with scans helps them live longer (Abstract, sentence 3). The team looked at how well current care works for two main types of lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 4). For one type, called non small cell, you may be cured if doctors find it early and remove the tumor with surgery and then give cancer drugs after (Abstract, sentence 4). A few people with more spread disease can get drugs and beam treatment first to shrink the tumor so it can be cut out (Abstract, sentence 5). Most people learn they have lung cancer when it is already far spread, and then a cure is not possible with today’s care (Abstract, sentence 6). For the other main type, small cell lung cancer, cure is only likely if it stays on one side of the chest and you get drug and beam treatment to the chest and head (Abstract, sentence 7). New drug types that aim at key cell paths are now in lab and human tests and may give better choices in the future (Abstract, sentence 9).
Full_Text_Summary_With_In_Text_Citations: This research looks at lung cancer, which is now the top cause of death from cancer in the world (Abstract, para. 1). It explains how lung cancer starts, how we find it, and what care can help at each stage (Body, para. 2). We need this study because many people smoke, and lung cancer rates and deaths are very high, while only about 14 out of 100 people are still alive five years after diagnosis (Body, para. 1). This work may help people who smoke now, people who used to smoke, and their families (Body, para. 3). The team reviewed large health reports and many past trials on lung cancer causes, tests, and treatments (Body, para. 1). They looked at surgery, drug care, and radiation, and also at newer “targeted” drugs that act on cancer cell growth signals (Body, para. 30). They found that surgery can cure some people when the cancer is found early, but most people are found late and cannot be cured with today’s tools (Abstract, para. 1). For these people, drug care and radiation can add a few months of life and ease pain and cough (Body, para. 20). New drugs like gefitinib and erlotinib can help some people after other drugs stop working, adding about two more months of life in some studies (Body, para. 30). These results support strong help to quit smoking and better early checks, plus careful use of surgery, drug care, and new targeted drugs to improve length and quality of life (Body, para. 5).
